title: Care is emerging as foundational social infrastructure: it converts household vulnerability into participation, security, and dignity
source_unit: United Nations Commission for Social Development, Eradicating poverty and ensuring dignity through resilient care and support systems (E/CN.5/2026/4)
geography: Global; national experiences and international evidence reviewed for the Commission for Social Development

observations.period: 2026; life-course definition of care and support systems

system_components.value: Legal and policy frameworks, services, financing, social and physical infrastructure, programmes, standards, training, governance, administration, and supportive norms

life_course_scope.value: Early childhood care and education, disability support, community and residential services, independent living, long-term care, and support for caregivers

participation_route.value: Care systems enable participation in education, employment, and social life while linking care-related needs to social protection

mechanism.value: Care is not only a household burden or a health service; it is infrastructure that determines whether people can participate in other institutions and markets

observations.method: UN Secretariat synthesis of international frameworks, available evidence, national experiences, and cross-sectoral policy considerations.
observations.uncertainty: The note is a policy synthesis rather than a harmonized global measurement system; definitions, coverage, and service quality vary across countries.
observations.subgroup: Children, older people, people with disabilities, caregivers, families facing care shocks, and workers dependent on care services.
observations.counterinterpretation: Families and communities provide substantial care outside formal systems, and formalization may not always improve cultural fit, autonomy, or dignity without user control.

observations.period: 2026; care systems and poverty, income, and social inclusion

social_returns.value: Accessible, affordable, quality care and support systems generate social and economic returns throughout the life course

poverty_route.value: Care systems can support poverty eradication and dignity by strengthening social protection, household resilience, and access to education and employment

shock_buffer.value: Care and support systems provide resilience during disruption while revealing pressures when coverage, workforce, financing, or infrastructure are under-resourced

mechanism.value: The same care need can become poverty, unpaid time, or exclusion when the system is absent, and capability when support is affordable and reachable

observations.method: UN review of evidence and policy experiences linking care systems to poverty, social protection, employment, education, and social inclusion.
observations.uncertainty: The note does not estimate a universal return on care investment or identify a single causal policy package that works across contexts.
observations.subgroup: Low-income households, families facing disability or ageing-related needs, children needing early support, and people whose employment depends on care availability.
observations.counterinterpretation: Care investment can be poorly targeted, fiscally unsustainable, or inaccessible if services are geographically concentrated or designed without affected people.

observations.period: 2026; gender, household responsibility, and labor-market participation

unpaid_care_distribution.value: When care systems are limited or uneven, unpaid care responsibilities fall disproportionately on women and girls

life_choice_effect.value: Unequal unpaid care affects income, security, education, employment, and participation in public life

co_responsibility.value: The UN system guidance frames care as a shared responsibility among genders, households, the State, markets, families, and communities

mechanism.value: Care time is a hidden allocation system: where responsibility is privatized, gender and household inequality compound even when formal rights are equal

observations.method: UN synthesis of care, gender, labor, social-protection, and social-development evidence.
observations.uncertainty: The note establishes a broad evidence and policy direction, not a new globally comparable estimate of unpaid-care hours or a causal gender-employment decomposition.
observations.subgroup: Women and girls, single-parent households, informal caregivers, families with disability or eldercare needs, and workers in low-paid care occupations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Redistributing care through services or paid work can create new burdens or reduce autonomy if caregivers and care recipients lack voice over service design.

persistent_gaps.value: Coverage, financing, workforce capacity, infrastructure, data, and coordination remain persistent constraints

policy_linkages.value: The note calls for integrating care with social protection, health, education, labor policy, and decent-work strategies

workforce_condition.value: Improving care work requires attention to decent work, training, standards, representation, and fair reward

data_and_governance.value: Data, governance, financing, and administrative mechanisms are part of the care system rather than after-the-fact evaluation tools

mechanism.value: Resilience depends on an integrated system that can finance, staff, reach, coordinate, and learn—not isolated family programs or facilities

observations.method: UN Secretariat review of policy options, good practices, global commitments, and system-wide guidance.
observations.uncertainty: The note identifies implementation requirements and examples but does not evaluate the effectiveness of each country practice or establish a common cost benchmark.
observations.subgroup: Care recipients, unpaid and paid caregivers, public agencies, employers, service providers, and communities with thin infrastructure or fiscal capacity.
observations.counterinterpretation: Integrated systems may increase administrative complexity; a smaller number of well-funded, locally accountable services could outperform broad coordination structures.

boundary: This record adds a global care-infrastructure route from life-course needs through household time, poverty, gender, work, social protection, public services, and dignity. It is a UN Secretariat policy note synthesizing evidence and good practices, not a harmonized global outcome dataset, respondent-level study, or causal evaluation of any care programme.
